replacements.old: Under exact replay with the same model, tokenizer, prompt configuration, and deterministic rank rule, the recovered rank satisfies \(\hat r_i=r_i\). The receiver can then replay the payload side context and reconstruct the hidden text token as \(\hat e_i=\operatorname{token}_{g_i}(\hat r_i)\). This is a 'same token length' arbitrary text baseline, one hidden text token determines one cover token. The construction shows that a rank sequence can be carried by generated text without directly emitting the hidden tokens. Direct application to cryptographic artifact strings (however can impose high rank pressure). Such strings are often poorly predicted by a language model, so their payload side tokens can occupy low probability, high rank positions, and selecting those same ranks under a cover prompt can degrade model likelihood and surface diagnostics even when recovery remains exact.
replacements.new: Under exact replay with the same model, tokenizer, prompt configuration and deterministic rank rule, the recovered rank satisfies \(\hat r_i=r_i\). The receiver then replays the payload context and reconstructs each hidden token as \(\hat e_i=\operatorname{token}_{g_i}(\hat r_i)\). This baseline carries one hidden-text token per cover token. Cryptographic artifact strings can occupy high ranks because their tokens are poorly predicted in the payload context. Transferring those ranks to a cover context can reduce token likelihood even when recovery remains exact. This motivates the bounded artifact codecs introduced below, which make the tradeoff between rank magnitude and cover length explicit.
replacements.reason: Repair the broken sentence and explain artifact-specific codecs.

replacements.old: The segmented multi-cover method extends RankCloak from one cover sequence to several shorter public messages. Long sequences of forced ranks can accumulate topic drift, formatting artifacts, or low-probability continuations. Segmentation restarts the cover context for each chunk, allowing the effect of distributing the payload across several messages to be measured without assuring the degree those messages are human-natural. The method is also useful analytically because it separates the payload-bearing forced span from the rest of the public message.
replacements.new: The segmented multi-cover method distributes one payload across several shorter public messages. Each segment restarts from a declared cover prompt, allowing the effects of context resets and forced-span length to be measured. The design also separates payload-bearing tokens from ordinary continuations, so payload efficiency and complete-message properties can be evaluated on their respective token spans.
replacements.reason: Describe segmentation directly.

replacements.old: A core component of this method is the forced span and tail separation. The payload is carried only by the forced span, while the tail is a greedy continuation whose effect on the complete public message is measured separately. This distinction prevents a misleading quality result, full-message diagnostics can change because of the non-payload tail even if the payload-bearing forced span remains low probability or exhibits surface artifacts. For that reason, the Results report forced span metrics and full message metrics separately.
replacements.new: Separate forced-span and full-message measurements distinguish the properties of payload-bearing tokens from those of the complete delivered text. Appending a greedy tail changes full-message averages without changing the forced tokens or adding payload capacity. The Results therefore report both scopes.
replacements.reason: State the measurement contribution.

replacements.old:
RankCloak provides a reproducible method for converting serialized cryptographic artifacts into language-model next-token ranks and realizing those ranks as cover text. Its representation choices expose a central tradeoff that direct subwords can be compact but leave rank pressure uncontrolled, whereas ASCII-byte and hex-nibble codecs bound the permitted rank by spending more forced positions. Segmentation redistributes those positions across contexts, and non-payload greedy continuations add non-payload length. The formal and empirical capacity relationships make these costs explicit rather than treating longer cover text as additional payload capacity.

The principal demonstrated transformation is that the recognizable surface representation of a synthetic cryptographic artifact can be absent from the generated cover while an authorized receiver reconstructs it under the supported shared configuration. In the saved-token condition, retaining the token stream isolates tokenization fidelity, but recovery still requires contextual rank reconstruction and codec inversion; ordinary visible-text transfer is the stricter and materially less reliable condition. Steganalysis addresses another endpoint: a detector can often flag the presence of encoding, weakening covert-channel stealth, without thereby observing the original artifact or recovering its serialization.

The intact-message follow-up measures a practical but explicitly automated endpoint. Under the lenient rubric, the panel accepts 90.3\% of encoded messages compared with 96.6\% of matched greedy controls. This quantifies acceptance despite minor awkwardness while retaining material disruptions and judge disagreements. It is neither a human reading rate nor evidence of indistinguishability. The comparison concerns complete delivered conditions, and length or content differences can contribute to the observed contrast.

The protocol comparisons explain part of the efficiency tradeoff. Larger segments reduce repeated tail overhead, while lead-ins change every subsequent forced-token history and worsened likelihood and length in the selected contrasts. A higher full-message likelihood can arise simply by adding greedy continuation tokens. It does not improve the forced span or increase its payload capacity.

Strict pre-feature component deduplication found zero leakage under the declared exact and character-\(n\)-gram rules, yet matched, unseen-family, and exact-model-aware detectors remained strong. Validation-frozen low-FPR results show that high ranking performance does not ensure threshold calibration after family or quantization shift. The human-authored comparison is informative but secondary: its high false-positive rates expose control-domain sensitivity and may reflect general machine-versus-human cues.

Entropy gating reduced text-only detectability at the cost of lower serialized-payload rates, longer covers and six strict-gate failures, while exact-model-aware detection remained strong. Quantization likewise preserved within-configuration saved-ID inversion without providing a statistically supported Q8 advantage in visible-text recovery. Together, the studies identify where configured artifact inversion succeeds and where transmission, efficiency and detection constrain its use. Historical conditional context gain adds evidence about local fixed-path compatibility, distinct from the primary intact-message acceptability endpoint.
replacements.new:
RankCloak makes the representation of cryptographic artifacts an explicit design choice in language-model information hiding. It combines exact serialization, contextual rank transfer and replay decoding with measurements of recovery, rate, text properties and detection. All 6,480 primary trials recovered the original bytes under the saved-token contract. This establishes a reproducible baseline for comparing how artifact representations influence generated cover text.

The codec comparison identifies a controllable efficiency tradeoff. Direct subword representations can be compact but have no fixed rank ceiling, whereas ASCII-byte and hex-nibble codecs bound rank magnitude by using more forced positions. Segmentation determines how those positions are distributed across contexts. Larger segments reduce repeated continuation overhead, while the tested lead-ins increased length and worsened likelihood. Separate forced-span and full-message measurements show how greedy continuations affect complete-message scores without changing payload-bearing tokens or increasing payload capacity.

The intact-message study extends evaluation from token-level diagnostics to automated contextual acceptability. Under a rubric accepting understandable text with minor awkwardness, the panel accepted 90.3\% of encoded messages and 96.6\% of matched greedy controls. The -6.3 percentage-point difference quantifies a remaining acceptability cost alongside the high acceptance level of encoded messages. These are model judgments of complete delivered conditions, with possible contributions from length and content differences; they do not establish human acceptance or indistinguishability. The historical likelihood analysis provides complementary evidence about local fixed-path compatibility.

The transport and detector studies distinguish recovery from stealth. Saved-token replay isolates the rank and codec operations, while visible-text replay exposes the consequences of retokenization and editing. Strong detection persisted after component deduplication and in held-family evaluations, providing a benchmark for recognizing encoding beyond visible artifact syntax. High ROC-AUC did not ensure stable low-FPR thresholds under distribution shift, and the human-authored controls exposed further domain sensitivity. Detecting encoding does not itself reconstruct the artifact, but it limits covert-channel stealth.

Entropy gating provides another measurable design tradeoff: text-only detection decreased as covers became longer and serialized-payload rates fell. The six strict-gate completion failures and continued strong model-aware detection identify costs of the tested thresholds. Both quantizations retained exact saved-ID recovery within their own configurations, while the visible-text comparison showed no statistically supported Q8 advantage. Together, these results provide a reference for designing and evaluating artifact-carrying text with explicit recovery, efficiency, acceptability and detection endpoints.
replacements.reason: Organize the contribution and experiment interpretations while retaining unfavorable outcomes.

replacements.old: RankCloak can encode sensitive looking artifacts, but it does not itself provide encryption, authentication, confidentiality or a cryptographic security proof. Protected payloads require an external cryptographic system and an explicit threat model. Perfect primary recovery was demonstrated under the preserved-token replay contract. Visible-text transmission and common transformations are fragile, and the tested perturbations do not establish broad edit robustness. Human-perceived naturalness, broad multilingual behavior, real-world deployment and performance across arbitrary future models or communication channels were not established. The contextual judges are small local instruction models, not human participants. Their generator assignments are not fully crossed, and reused greedy controls form a fixed reference set. The selected payloads exclude the earlier scored cohort. Acceptance under this rubric neither proves indistinguishability nor isolates a causal effect of an encoding boundary. The historical fragment assays and their unsuccessful semantic control checks are retained in Supplementary Note S17. Detector performance is limited to the evaluated corpus. Detailed boundaries appear in Supplementary Table S17 and Notes S16 through S20.
replacements.new:
RankCloak is a representation layer for cryptographic artifacts. Encryption and authentication must be supplied by an external cryptographic system under an explicit threat model; the carrier itself provides no confidentiality or cryptographic security guarantee. Exact recovery was demonstrated with preserved tokens and matching configurations. Visible-text and transformed-text results show that reliable edited-text transport remains an open problem. Detector findings apply to the evaluated corpus, and operational deployment, broad multilingual text quality and generalization to arbitrary models or channels remain untested.

The contextual study measures automated judgments from local instruction models. Human perception and indistinguishability were not measured. Judges and generators are not fully crossed, greedy controls are reused as a fixed reference set, and the selected payloads exclude the earlier scored cohort. The estimates condition on complete ratings; missingness sensitivity is reported in Supplementary Note S20. The comparison evaluates delivered messages without isolating a causal boundary effect. Supplementary Note S17 retains both unsuccessful semantic control checks and the complementary likelihood analysis; Table S17 and Notes S16 through S20 give the detailed scope of the evidence.
replacements.reason: Organize limitations by security, transport and inference.

replacements.old: Small configuration changes have no universal recovery rate. The conditional rank-agreement argument in Supplementary Note S19 makes these dependencies explicit without assigning a recovery rate from a version label.
replacements.new: Reliable replay requires compatible token boundaries, rank orderings and payload-position rules. A tokenizer update can split or merge tokens, shifting saved offsets and later conditioning; weight or quantization changes can reorder candidates even on an identical received history. Gate disagreement changes which positions consume payload digits. Supplementary Note S19 formalizes these dependencies through conditional rank agreement. Recovery under a changed configuration therefore requires direct verification rather than inference from a version label.
replacements.reason: Frame compatibility as a concrete requirement.

replacements.old: The main Algorithms 1 and 2 define the saved-token exact-copy condition. In the experiments, payload-bearing token IDs were retained in the generation records and supplied to the decoder to hold tokenization and history fixed; the decoder nevertheless recomputes contextual ranks and performs codec inversion. A token-preserving channel could transmit that exact stream, whereas detokenized-text replay renders the visible message, invokes the embedded tokenizer again after stripping one automatically inserted BOS token when applicable, and applies the saved forced offsets. This boundary rule is a diagnostic; it does not search for alternate tokenizations or infer a payload span from prose. Transformed-text replay applies one frozen perturbation before this step, and cross-model replay uses a different declared model/tokenizer pair. Thus retaining IDs is neither irrelevant nor evidence that a separate secret copy of them must be transmitted for every message; it defines one evaluated recovery condition distinct from ordinary visible-text and transformed-text delivery.
replacements.new: Main Algorithms 1 and 2 evaluate saved-token recovery. Retained payload-bearing token IDs hold tokenization and history fixed while the decoder recomputes contextual ranks and inverts the codec. A token-preserving channel could transmit this stream directly. Visible-text replay instead renders the message and reapplies the embedded tokenizer, stripping one automatically inserted BOS token when applicable before using the saved forced offsets. This diagnostic applies the declared offsets without searching alternative tokenizations or inferring boundaries from prose. Transformed-text replay adds one frozen perturbation, and cross-model replay uses a different declared model/tokenizer pair. These conditions separate rank and codec recovery from the additional requirements of ordinary text delivery.
replacements.reason: Explain recovery conditions directly.
